scenes.headline: Type Hints & the typing Module
scenes.subtitle: Documenting and checking types statically
scenes.narration: Type hints make your code self-documenting and let static analysis tools catch a whole class of bugs before you ever run the program.

scenes.headline: Basic annotations
scenes.narration: Parameter annotations follow a colon after the name, so amounts is declared as a list of floats. The return type follows an arrow after the parameter list, here promising a float. Variables can be annotated the same way, as name and retries show. These hints instantly tell any reader, and any tool, what shape of data each name is meant to hold.

scenes.headline: Common typing tools
scenes.narration: Optional marks a value that may legitimately be None, forcing callers to consider the empty case. Union, or the newer pipe syntax, allows a value to be one of several types. The built-in generics like list and dict let you specify what a container holds. And richer constructs such as Callable, Any, and TypedDict describe functions, escape hatches, and structured dictionaries respectively.

scenes.headline: Optional and generics
scenes.code:
from typing import Optional

def find_user(uid: int) -> Optional[dict]:
    row = db.get(uid)
    return row  # dict or None
scenes.narration: This function returns an Optional dict, which is shorthand for a dict or None. That single annotation communicates that a lookup might miss, and a type checker will then flag any caller that uses the result without first handling the None case. Making absence explicit in the signature prevents a very common category of crash.

scenes.headline: Hints vs runtime
scenes.narration: Type hints are a static tool: checkers like mypy verify them and editors use them for autocomplete, all without adding any runtime cost. At runtime, though, CPython simply ignores them and does not enforce a thing. So if you need actual runtime validation of incoming data, reach for a library like pydantic rather than expecting the hints alone to protect you.

scenes.text: Type hints are documentation and tooling, not runtime checks. Run mypy in CI to catch errors early.
scenes.narration: Annotate your public functions and run mypy in continuous integration, and your type hints become a genuine safety net rather than mere documentation.
